title: Franks
description: Germanic people from the Lower Rhine
wiki_lead:
The Franks (Latin: Franci) were a Western European people who began in the third century as a group of Germanic tribes near the Lower Rhine River, but gradually became a multilingual, Catholic Christian people, who controlled a large territory both inside and outside the former Roman Empire. Much of what is now  the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, France, and in a broader sense much of the population of medieval Western Europe, could eventually be described as Frankish, depending on the context.
Pre-existing Germanic tribes such as the Bructeri and Chattuari began being referred to as Franks during the crisis of the 3rd century, when Rome lost control of regions near the lower Rhine, within the Roman province of Germania Inferior. The Rhine was a militarized border defended by the Romans, and the Frankish tribes had been living across the Rhine under Roman hegemony for centuries, under other tribal names. During the crisis they made frequent incursions, and in some cases settled areas on the Roman side. Despite the reassertion of Roman authority in the 4th century, Franks continued to live semi-independently on both sides of the Rhine, while the Romans came to agreements with them, recruiting large numbers of Frankish soldiers, some of whom achieved high imperial rank. 
After the Roman administration of Britain and northern Gaul eventually broke down once more in the fifth century, it was the Franks who attempted to defend the Roman border in 406 when a large-scale Rhine crossing was made by Alans and Vandals from eastern Europe. Frankish kings subsequently divided up Germania Inferior between them, and at least one, Chlodio, also began to rule more Romanized populations to the south, in what is now northern France. In 451, Frankish groups participated on both sides in the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, where Attila and his allies were defeated by a Roman-led alliance of various peoples established in Gaul. By the early 6th century, the whole of Gaul north of the Loire, and all the Frankish kingdoms, were united within the kingdom of the Frank Clovis I, the founder of the Merovingian dynasty. By building upon the basis of this empire, the subsequent Frankish dynasty, the Carolingians, eventually came to be seen as the new emperors of Western Europe in 800, when Charlemagne was crowned by the pope.
As the original Frankish communities merged into others, the term Frank lost its original meaning. In 870, the Frankish realm was permanently divided between western and eastern kingdoms, which were the predecessors of the later Kingdom of France and Holy Roman Empire respectively. These two large regions contained two core Frankish regions, known at first as Neustria and Austrasia, as well as regions associated with non-Frankish identities. The Latin term Franci, and equivalents in other languages, came to refer especially to the people of the Kingdom of France. However, in various historical contexts, such as during the medieval crusades, not only the French, but also people from neighbouring regions in Western Europe, continued to be referred to collectively as Franks. The crusades in particular had a lasting impact on the use of Frank-related names, which are now used generically for all Western Europeans in many non-European languages.

Meaning of the term "Franks"


Etymology
While the original meaning of the word is not certain, it is commonly believed to have a Germanic etymology. Following the precedents of Edward Gibbon and Jacob Grimm, the name of the Franks was traditionally linked to Old French franc, and related terms such as the English adjective frank, meaning "free". The latter term is however derived from the term Frank itself, as it referred to their free status. Similarly, the word has been connected to a Germanic word for "javelin", reflected in words such as Old English franca or Old Norse frakka, but these terms possibly also derive from the name of the Franks, as the name of a Frankish weapon. grok_lead: The Franks were a confederation of West Germanic tribes that first appeared in Roman records during the 3rd century CE along the lower Rhine River, initially serving as foederati allies to the Roman Empire before expanding southward into Gaul amid its collapse. Under the leadership of Clovis I in the late 5th century, the Franks achieved unification of their disparate groups through military conquests, defeating Roman remnants and rival Germanic kingdoms such as the Visigoths at the Battle of VouillÃ© in 507 CE, while Clovis's conversion to Catholic Christianityâdistinct from the Arianism prevalent among other Germanic rulersâfacilitated alliances with the Gallo-Roman population and the Church. This established the Merovingian dynasty, which ruled a kingdom encompassing much of modern France, Belgium, and western Germany, blending Germanic customs with Roman administrative traditions. The Merovingians' power waned by the 8th century due to internal divisions and ineffective rule, paving the way for the rise of the Carolingian mayors of the palace, culminating in Pepin the Short's deposition of the last Merovingian king in 751 CE and the establishment of the Carolingian dynasty with papal sanction. Under Charlemagne, crowned Emperor by Pope Leo III in 800 CE, the Frankish Empire reached its zenith, extending from the Pyrenees to the Elbe River and incorporating diverse peoples through conquest, missionary activity, and legal reforms that emphasized Christian unity and feudal structures. The empire's division under the Treaty of Verdun in 843 CE among Charlemagne's grandsons laid the groundwork for the distinct trajectories of France and Germany, marking the Franks' enduring causal role in shaping medieval Europe's political geography despite linguistic assimilation into Romance and other vernaculars over time.
